MIDAS – introduced as “a statewide database of current and future time-dependent rates, GHG emissions, and California ISO Flex Alert Signals” (Herter and Situ 2021) – was designed to be the principal tool supporting the 2022 LMS, which was already being developed through a CEC Rulemaking.24 The idea was that MIDAS would provide real-time signals to end-use devices to shift or reduce load through the assistance of automation technology. The 2022 LMS amendments build on a long tradition of load management regulations by the CEC, dating back to 1979 (see the California Code of Regulations (CCR), Title 20, §§ 1621- 1625). These earliest regulations “compelled the implementation of marginal cost pricing, industrial time-of-use (TOU) rates, commercial building audits, and residential load control programs” (Herter and Situ 2021). The CEC Final Staff Report, Analysis of Potential Amendments to the Load Management Standards (i.e. Herter and Situ 2021), traces the history of CEC policy actions since 1979, which it states has resulted in “each of California’s roughly 70 load serving entities (LSEs) offer[ing] their own version of load management program portfolios, largely populated by incentive programs that reward participants for load shed.” Herter and Situ (2021) catalogue several problems with this situation, including: (1) most programs cannot shift load “to absorb plentiful renewable supplies” because they focus on emergency curtailment and specify fixed seasons of the year, days of a week, or times of day; (2) utility customers who are not able to participate in programs because their loads are too small or they have insufficient usage of end uses like air conditioning and electric water heating cannot “benefit directly from participation, [but] they are still required to contribute through rate charges to cover the costs of running the program”; (3) “utilities incur high costs from incentive programs,” for example, by “developing and seeking approval, marketing, contracting with participants, and maintaining back-office systems”; (4) customer enrollment requires people to research and consider “a cornucopia of offerings that have different incentives, options, and requirements … coordinate installation of technologies, keep track of their event performance to avoid steep noncompliance penalties, and coordinate their managed energy use with their time- varying energy and demand rates; (5) “pay-for-performance” programs that “reward customers for their load impacts relative to an estimated baseline” benefit “inefficient customers more than the efficient ones”; and (6) most residential load control programs have limited appeal because utility-installed and controlled air-conditioning automation do not always allow opt-outs, and when they do they are often “tied to penalties or constrained to a certain number per year.” Herter and Situ (2021) states that “time-dependent rates have long been considered a more efficient alternative to incentive programs” and can overcome many of these issues.
